issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette:
Karim, a 75-year-old Middle Eastern widower who had spent most of his life as a sculptor, came for help months after a life-threatening accident that had overturned the rhythm of his days. He had been in his workshop alone when a heavy slab of stone slipped from a hoist and pinned him hard enough to leave him unable to move, his chest compressed and his body failing him in a way he still described with disbelief. He remembered the smell of dust, the panic of not being able to draw a full breath, and the humiliating certainty that he might die surrounded by the unfinished forms he had been shaping for decades. Afterward, ordinary tasks in the studio felt altered. Lifting a chisel, bending over a workbench, or even standing too long at the marble saw could bring back the same jolt of fear, because his own body now felt like the thing he could least trust.

In the weeks that followed, Karim began to interpret the accident as proof that something fundamental had changed in him. He had come to believe that his body was unreliable, that it could fail without warning, and that the injury had left him permanently damaged. What frightened him most was not only the memory of the stone and the crushing weight, but the conviction that he had been physically changed for the worse and that this damage would never fully go away. He would pause in the middle of a sculpting session and place a hand against his ribs or shoulder, checking for a tightness, a weakness, some sign that the body beneath his clothes was giving out again. These thoughts did not stay abstract for long; because he believed his body could no longer be trusted, he became preoccupied with why the event had happened to him and what it meant about the rest of his life. He replayed the accident over and over, trying to make sense of it, asking himself whether age had made him careless, whether he should have known the hoist was unsafe, whether the universe had singled him out for a loss he could not undo.

That search for meaning threaded through the rest of his suffering. Karim found himself thinking about the accident while waking, while sitting at breakfast, and while arranging tools in the studio, as if understanding the event might somehow protect him from its return. But each time he noticed a twinge in his back, a strain in his chest, or a flutter of fatigue after a day of work, the meaning he assigned was the same: his body was not dependable anymore, and another sudden catastrophe could happen just as easily. Those appraisals kept his attention fixed on physical danger. He monitored his body constantly, scanning for pain, unsteadiness, or any sign that he was pushing himself too far. He began avoiding physical stress with increasing determination. He stopped taking on heavy stone commissions, let younger assistants handle lifting, and limited his time in the workshop when the work required sustained standing or force. At home, even carrying groceries or climbing stairs became deliberate and cautious, because exertion itself felt like an invitation to another collapse.

The more Karim tried to protect himself, the smaller his life became. He turned down projects that he would once have accepted without hesitation, and his studio, once a place of absorbed concentration, became a place where he measured each movement against the possibility of injury. His daughter noticed that he was no longer eager to demonstrate new pieces or invite colleagues over, and Karim quietly withdrew rather than explain how embarrassing it felt to fear his own strength. He still spoke often about the accident, but now it was less an account than an attempt to solve an unsolved question: why had this happened to him, and how could a body that had betrayed him be trusted again? Even when he told himself to slow down, the checking never really stopped. He would flex his hands, press along his torso, and listen to his breathing, as though vigilance might reveal a hidden sign before danger struck. By the time he sought treatment, his symptoms had become hard to ignore. He was exhausted by the constant mental effort of watching his body, and he was increasingly alarmed by how much he avoided work that required any strain. What finally brought him in was the fear that if he kept living this way, he would lose not only his health but the sculpting life that had given his widowhood structure and meaning, and he hoped for some way to believe that his body was still his to use.
